sources.title: Hackensack Meridian Health: does toothpaste help with acne?

title: What you eat causes acne

claims.claim: Sugar and high-glycemic foods worsen acne
claims.truth: Studies link high-glycemic diets to more acne in some people, and a few trials found improvement on low-glycemic diets. It's a contributing factor, not the main cause.
Skim milk shows the most consistent link in observational studies; cheese and yogurt less so. Cutting dairy helps some people, not all.

sources.title: Diet and acne: a systematic review (PubMed)

title: Tea tree oil treats acne

claims.claim: Tea tree oil helps mild acne
claims.truth: In a trial of 124 people, 5% tea tree gel reduced spots, more slowly than 5% benzoyl peroxide but with less dryness. It's a reasonable gentle option for mild acne.

claims.claim: Neat tea tree oil works better
claims.truth: Undiluted tea tree oil can burn and cause allergic rashes, especially when old and oxidised. Use about 5%.

sources.title: Bassett et al. 1990, tea tree oil vs benzoyl peroxide (PubMed)

title: Minoxidil works for women's thinning hair

claims.claim: Minoxidil regrows hair in female pattern hair loss
claims.truth: A Cochrane review found topical minoxidil clearly better than placebo for women's pattern hair loss. It takes 4 to 6 months, shedding can increase at first, and results stop if you stop using it.

sources.title: van Zuuren et al. 2016, Cochrane review: interventions for female pattern hair loss

title: Rosemary oil works as well as minoxidil

claims.claim: Rosemary oil regrows hair like minoxidil
claims.truth: One small 6-month trial (100 men) found diluted rosemary oil and 2% minoxidil gave similar small gains, with less scalp itch on rosemary. It hasn't been repeated, used the weaker 2% minoxidil and had no placebo group, so it's a hint, not proof.
Essential oils need diluting (about 1 to 2% in a carrier oil or shampoo) or they can irritate the scalp.

sources.title: Panahi et al. 2015, SkinMed (trial record)
Lab Muffin: what the rosemary study actually shows

title: Coconut oil before washing protects hair

claims.claim: Coconut oil reduces damage from washing
claims.truth: In a lab study, coconut oil used before and after washing reduced protein loss from both damaged and undamaged hair; sunflower and mineral oil didn't. Coconut oil's small fatty acid (lauric acid) can get inside the hair shaft.
In the same study only coconut oil reduced protein loss. Other oils still help as a coating against tangles and friction.

sources.title: Rele & Mohile 2003, J Cosmet Sci (PubMed)

title: Scalp massage makes hair thicker

claims.truth: A tiny study (9 men, 4 minutes a day for 24 weeks, with a massage device) found slightly thicker hairs but no change in hair count. Promising and free, but very little evidence.

sources.title: Koyama et al. 2016, Eplasty (PubMed)

title: Castor oil (including Jamaican black castor oil) grows hair

claims.truth: There are no good human studies showing castor oil grows hair. It is a thick, sealing oil that can make hair feel softer and reduce breakage, which helps you keep length.

claims.claim: Castor oil is harmless on hair
claims.truth: Usually, but heavy castor oil use has been linked to rare, sudden matting (felting) of long hair. Use a little and wash it out well.

sources.title: Dermatology Times: can castor oil really grow hair?

title: Biotin supplements grow hair

claims.claim: Biotin makes healthy hair grow faster
claims.truth: Biotin only helped in people who were actually deficient or had specific conditions, which is rare. There's no evidence it helps people with normal levels.
It's not toxic, but high doses can throw off blood tests, including thyroid and heart (troponin) tests. Tell your doctor if you take it.

sources.title: Patel et al. 2017, Skin Appendage Disorders (review)

title: Low iron causes hair shedding

claims.claim: Low iron is linked to hair loss in women
claims.truth: Studies link low iron stores (ferritin) to non-scarring hair loss in women, though not every study agrees. If you're shedding a lot, a ferritin blood test is worth asking for.
Only if a test shows you're low. Too much iron is harmful, and supplements can upset the stomach.

sources.title: Iron deficiency and nonscarring alopecia in women: systematic review and meta-analysis (PubMed)
Trost et al. 2006, JAAD (PubMed)

title: Tight braids, ponytails and glued wigs thin your edges

claims.claim: Tension hairstyles can cause hair loss
claims.truth: Traction alopecia comes from repeated pulling: tight braids, locs, weaves, ponytails and glued units, especially at the hairline. Early on it's reversible if the tension stops.
Long-standing traction can scar the follicles and become permanent. Loosen styles at the first sign of bumps, soreness or thinning, and see a dermatologist if edges don't recover.

sources.title: Billero & Miteva 2018, Traction alopecia: the root of the problem

title: Rice water makes hair grow faster

claims.truth: No human studies show rice water speeds growth. The evidence is a lab study showing it can make hair smoother (less surface friction), which may mean fewer tangles and less breakage.

claims.claim: It's good for every hair type
claims.truth: Its starch and small protein can leave low-porosity or protein-sensitive hair stiff and brittle. Rinse it out well and stop if hair feels hard or snaps.

sources.title: Inamasu et al. 2010, J Cosmet Sci (rice water and hair)

title: Rosemary butter or infused oil grows hair

claims.truth: The only human study used rosemary essential oil on the scalp for 6 months in 100 men, compared with low-strength minoxidil, without a placebo group. A butter or oil with rosemary steeped in it is much weaker and has never been tested.
Coconut oil soaks into the hair fibre and cuts protein loss during washing, so lengths break less. That's a real benefit, but it means keeping length, not new growth.

sources.title: Panahi et al. 2015, SkinMed (trial record)
Rele & Mohile 2003, J Cosmet Sci (PubMed)

title: Onion oil grows baby hairs, and Redensyl is clinically proven

claims.truth: One small 2002 study used raw onion juice on people with alopecia areata (patchy, autoimmune hair loss). It hasn't been tested on everyday thinning or pattern loss, and nobody has tested onion cooked into oil.
Its studies are small and run or paid for by the company that sells it. Independent trials are missing.

claims.claim: Less shedding after a few weeks means regrowth
claims.truth: Hair grows about 1 cm a month. Less hair in the drain after weeks of oiling usually means less breakage. Minoxidil is the over-the-counter option with solid proof.

sources.title: Dr. Jeff Donovan (dermatologist): onion extracts for alopecia areata
American Academy of Dermatology: hair loss diagnosis and treatment

title: Biotin in shampoo strengthens hair

claims.truth: Biotin helped hair only in people who were actually deficient, which is rare. In a shampoo it rinses away within a minute anyway.
High-dose biotin supplements can skew blood tests, including thyroid and troponin (heart attack) tests. Tell your doctor if you take them.

claims.claim: Something in the shampoo can strengthen hair
claims.truth: Hydrolyzed proteins (keratin, rice, wheat) coat hair and make it feel stronger while they're on it.

sources.title: Patel et al. 2017, Skin Appendage Disorders (review)
FDA: biotin interference with lab tests

title: Korean scalp serums with PDRN and exosomes regrow hair

claims.truth: The human study on PDRN for hair loss injected it into the scalp together with platelet-rich plasma. There's no good evidence that a serum you brush on gets the same effect.
The US FDA has approved no exosome product for any use and has warned consumers about unapproved ones. Plant exosomes in cosmetics have almost no human data.

Minoxidil has solid proof for pattern thinning. What people love about these serums is the brush tip, which makes daily use easy. Viral serums are often faked, so buy from the brand or a major retailer.

sources.title: Platelet-rich plasma and PDRN injections for female pattern hair loss, 2015 (PubMed)
FDA consumer alert: stem cell and exosome products
van Zuuren et al. 2016, Cochrane review: interventions for female pattern hair loss

title: Amla, bhringraj and brahmi make hair grow fast

claims.truth: The growth evidence comes from studies in rats and mice, not people.
There are no good human studies.
As oils and masks they condition hair and may cut breakage, which helps you keep length. Healthy growth still comes from a clean scalp, low tension and gentle handling.

sources.title: Hair growth promoting activity of Eclipta alba in male albino rats, 2008 (PubMed)
Comparative hair restorer efficacy of medicinal herbs on nude mice, 2014

title: Black sesame and honey reverse grey hair

claims.truth: Grey hair comes mostly from genes and age. A 2024 review says greying usually advances gradually and is permanent, with only occasional reports of colour coming back on its own.

claims.claim: Diet has nothing to do with it
claims.truth: Early greying has been linked in small studies to low vitamin B12, iron, copper, vitamin D or an underactive thyroid. A doctor can test for these. Sesame is a fine snack unless you're allergic.
Henna and indigo stain grey hair. They cover it; they don't reverse it.

sources.title: Poonia & Bhalla 2024, Premature graying of hair: a comprehensive review

title: Thickening shampoos and scalp serums grow thicker hair

claims.truth: They coat and swell existing strands for a fuller feel until your next wash. They don't create new hairs.

claims.claim: Peptide and caffeine serums regrow hair
claims.truth: The evidence is modest and mostly paid for by the brands.
Minoxidil is the proven over-the-counter option for pattern thinning. Sudden shedding after stress, illness, surgery or a new baby usually settles within months. A doctor can check iron and thyroid.

sources.title: American Academy of Dermatology: hair loss diagnosis and treatment
American Academy of Dermatology: female pattern hair loss
van Zuuren et al. 2016, Cochrane review: interventions for female pattern hair loss

title: Hair growth multivitamins grew my hair long

claims.truth: A 2019 review found that vitamins and minerals help hair only when you're short on one. A blood test can show iron, vitamin D or zinc levels. Taking more than you need doesn't add growth, and too much vitamin A or selenium can cause hair loss.
High-dose biotin can trigger breakouts in some people, and it skews thyroid and heart blood tests. Tell your doctor before any blood work.

sources.title: Almohanna et al. 2019, The role of vitamins and minerals in hair loss (PubMed)
FDA: biotin interference with lab tests

title: Ayurvedic herbs stop postpartum hair loss

claims.truth: Shedding a few months after birth is normal. Hairs that pregnancy hormones held in the growing phase fall at the same time. It peaks about 4 months after birth and most women are back to their usual thickness by the baby's first birthday. Masks and rinses add shine but can't stop it.
Gentle handling and loose styles help. If shedding goes past a year or comes out in patches, ask a doctor to check iron and thyroid.

sources.title: American Academy of Dermatology: hair loss in new moms

title: BUR BUR is a DHT blocker that stops shedding and grows new hair in 3 weeks

claims.truth: Nettle's DHT evidence is for nettle root taken by mouth, in prostate studies. This product uses nettle leaf on the scalp.
Burdock may soothe a dry, itchy scalp, but there's no evidence it grows hair. Bakuchiol and vitamin C are face ingredients with no hair-growth data.

Hair grows about 1 cm a month, so real regrowth takes months to see. Less hair in the drain after 3 weeks usually means less breakage or a calmer scalp. For thinning that worries you, minoxidil has the evidence. A homemade version is in Recipes.

sources.title: American Academy of Dermatology: hair loss diagnosis and treatment
van Zuuren et al. 2016, Cochrane review: interventions for female pattern hair loss

title: Saudi "brightening" stores, checked (Super Girl, Skincare Bakry, Whitura, Bahati, Freshes)
body: None of the store pages list ingredients except one: Skincare Bakry's Snowhite brightening soap lists sorbitol, glycerin, lye, shea, propylene glycol, water, olive oil, lemon oil, kojic acid, vitamin C, vitamin E and retinol. Honest read: in a soap that's rinsed off, kojic acid, vitamin C and retinol mostly break down or wash away; lemon oil can irritate; and "use every other day to rest the skin" is a sign it's harsher than a normal soap. The warnings (not for pregnancy, eczema or after laser) are sensible. Super Girl's 7-piece bundle (199 SAR): snow white mix, lightening soap, herbal coffee scrub, body cream, Moroccan soap, tebrima and Sudanese dilka, with no ingredients, directions or warnings on the page. Treat unlisted "snow white" and lightening mixes as unsafe until you see a full list; homemade-style lightening products in the Gulf and Africa have repeatedly been found with mercury, hydroquinone and strong steroids, which cause thinning skin, stretch marks and dark patches. "Safe in pregnancy" (Whitura) with no ingredient list is not a claim you can trust. Bahati's guarana-caffeine scrub and green tea neem soap are ordinary, low-risk body products. Freshes makes scrubs and soaps; no product details are listed. Check SFDA registration on the SFDA website before trusting "SFDA licensed".

title: More from this batch

claims.claim: TCM: no ice water on the face, wear socks, cover the lower back, drink warm water
claims.truth: cold splashes don't damage a healthy skin barrier (they cause brief redness); a chilled gua sha is just gentler. Warm feet and warm drinks feel good, but "cold invading the body" and "Kidney Yang" aren't measurable.

mostly hydrators, fine, but Ashirira "foot detox" patches turn dark from sweat reacting with the pad (they do the same on a damp cloth), not toxins; exosome, PDRN and copper peptide creams have weak proof.
right diagnosis (ends breaking, not slow growth), but braids aren't the cause; tight, heavy or long-left braids are. Low-tension braids with moisturised ends retain length well.

claims.claim: e.l.f. Never Thirsty and slip conditioners
claims.truth: slip comes from conditioning agents (behentrimonium, cetrimonium, silicones), not price; affordable is fine. For very damaged hair: trim the worst ends, bond or protein treatment every 2 to 4 weeks, low heat with protectant.
mostly cornstarch or talc with strong fragrance; skip on broken skin and don't inhale clouds of it.

title: This batch, checked

claims.truth: oil and sugar scrubs don't grow mould on their own; wet hands, shower water, shower gel, castile soap, rose water and kitchen extracts add water and let it in. Glycerin is a humectant, not a preservative.

claims.claim: Whipped Ethiopian butter with coffee and peppermint
claims.truth: "3 inches in 6 weeks" is impossible; hair grows about ½ inch a month. One commenter says it cut her hair; heavy dairy butter plus vigorous handling can tangle and break coily ends. The commenter who said genetics matter most is right; butters help keep length, not make it.

claims.claim: Ann Wood's long hair (no heat, no colour, good food, masks)
claims.truth: sensible: protein, iron, zinc and omega-3 matter if you're low; rosemary oil has one small study; castor oil has none for growth but conditions; coconut oil reduces protein loss when used before washing.

"Products support, how you handle your hair decides" and "heat isn't the problem" (with a protectant and moderate temperature) are both true. Bond builders (K18, Olaplex) help chemically or heat-damaged hair.
untrue (acne is common everywhere); the drink is healthy, and the gut-skin link is real but early research.
a few small studies show modest effects in stress tests; it's not a hormone treatment. High doses can cause stomach upset and kidney stones in some people.

title: Shaving, eczema and 4C hair: this batch, checked

claims.claim: 4-step shave (butter, razor, after-shave oil, ingrown oil)
claims.truth: sound. Oil goes on after shaving, as the creator says, and light oils don't stain clothes once absorbed. Commenters with hives or razor burn on their thighs usually need a sharper blade, fewer passes and no fragrance there. Glycolic for strawberry legs works, on non-shave nights.

claims.claim: Body scrub: mix, damp skin, gentle massage, rinse, moisturise
claims.truth: right, and so is "don't scrub aggressively".

the creator's advice is good: no exfoliating, fading or sealing products on active eczema, keep it moist and rinse off irritants. But "don't take prednisone" is wrong as blanket advice; a doctor-prescribed course is sometimes needed for severe flares, while daily steroid pills long-term are what doctors avoid. Food allergies cause eczema only in some people, mostly children; cut foods only after testing. Colloidal silver has no good evidence for eczema and can turn skin permanently blue-grey (argyria) if taken. Pure glycerin soap and shea butter are reasonable for some.

an honest one. "Grease and butter seal, they don't grow" and "supporting the scalp isn't a fix" are exactly right. Clarifying every wash suits heavy butter and grease users, but it's drying for most, so every 2 to 4 weeks is typical. Nizoral (ketoconazole) is the medicated shampoo for flaking and itch. Of her scalp serums, minoxidil is the only one with strong proof for thinning; rosemary, peptides and caffeine have weak proof.

title: This batch, checked

claims.claim: "Fast whole-body whitening" with Ordinary 7% toner, the AHA 30% peel, Dove scrub and Johnson's oil
claims.truth: the same dangerous three-exfoliants combo as before, now sold as whitening. It risks burns and dark marks, and 美白 creams promising fast results can hide mercury.

claims.claim: Glycolic acid + vitamin C for a glow
claims.truth: both work, but layering them on the same night stings; vitamin C in the morning, glycolic at night.
right ingredients (glycolic, urea, retinol), but start one at a time; a monthly hammam is fine but not required.

claims.claim: Zinc cream every night (Uriage, Avène Cicalfate, La Roche-Posay Cicaplast)
claims.truth: great for irritated or over-exfoliated skin and dry patches; on acne-prone skin a thick layer can clog, so use it as a spot or short-term repair, not forever.

it can work for some coily hair with very little product, but sebum doesn't "balance pH" and water can't remove sunscreen, pollution or oil-based products; build-up and odour are common, as commenters say. A gentle shampoo every 1 to 2 weeks is the middle ground.
real for hard water and chlorine; use every 2 to 4 weeks.
warmth helps conditioners spread, but "penetrating" is overstated.
use lighter, water-based products, apply to wet hair and use gentle heat; heavy butters sit on top.

claims.claim: Camille Rose chebe butter, Blue Magic
claims.truth: chebe's benefit is coating and length retention; Blue Magic is petrolatum, which seals but builds up, so clarify more often.
true and cheap; dilute it.
nice polish; "AHA" from tamarind in a rinse-off scrub is minor.

Komfymed and Voolga "medical" sodium hyaluronate masks are hydrogel dressings, soothing after treatments; recombinant collagen has early evidence, mostly from brands. Guyu's glabridin (licorice) has small studies for dark spots. Fulqun targets acne. Dabao SOD lotion is a cheap, decent basic moisturiser; "SOD antioxidant" adds little.
modern clean musks are synthetic and smell like clean skin, not animal; fragrance should go around, not on, intimate areas.

title: Night shower order: double cleansing, hair first, damp skin

claims.truth: true, especially if you get back or chest acne or KP; conditioner and styling residue rinse down your back and can clog pores, so wash and condition hair first, then cleanse your body.

useful only on days with sweat, sunscreen or heavy body products; one wash with a gentle bar or wash (like Dove) used twice is enough, and the creator is right not to double cleanse with antibacterial soap daily, as it dries skin.
true for lotions, oils and butters (they trap the water), but not antiperspirant or acids like glycolic, which sting more on wet skin.

claims.claim: Glycolic body products at night plus sunscreen on exposed skin by day
claims.truth: correct.
bond repair helps bleached or chemically damaged hair; for virgin hair a regular conditioner does the job.
4711 cologne, zinc creams like Penaten and Kneipp baths are simple, decades-old formulas that work; homeopathic remedies and "bitters for skin" have no evidence beyond placebo.

title: Bath salts, bath oils and "medicated" bath powders: what they actually do
body: Kneipp (founded by priest Sebastian Kneipp in the 1890s) built its brand on hydrotherapy: water, plants, movement, food and balance. Alternating warm and cold water and a regular bath ritual do help people relax and sleep; the herbal oils add scent and soften skin. Japanese bath powders (Matsukiyo, Bathclin) use hot-spring salts (sodium sulfate, sodium bicarbonate) and are legally "quasi-drugs" for stiffness and feeling cold: the salts make the bath feel silkier and the warmth last a little longer after you get out, but the warm water does most of the work. Carbonated tablets are the one type with a measurable effect: CO2 dilates small skin blood vessels at high concentrations. Claims you can ignore: "detox", "remineralising", and magnesium absorbed through skin. Use 25 to 30 g of powder per full tub, not a whole scoop, and buy single sachets before an 800 g tub.

title: Night shower routine tips, a scalp tonic, HA powder and milky oats, checked

claims.claim: Wait 15 to 20 minutes before bed after layering body products
claims.truth: sensible; less ends up on your sheets.

claims.claim: Antiperspirant at night on dry skin
claims.truth: true and backed by studies; sweat glands are quieter, so the aluminium plugs the ducts better, and it still works after a morning shower. On damp skin it stings and works less.
(an exfoliating night, a retinol night, then barrier-cream nights): a good way to use strong actives without irritation.
"cADPR" is a brand story with no independent hair trials; the comb tip just makes it easier to apply. For real shedding, check iron and consider minoxidil.

claims.claim: High molecular weight hyaluronic acid powder
claims.truth: the demo is right: HA thickens water and holds moisture on the skin's surface for a temporarily plumper look. Use 0.1 to 1%; more turns sticky and can pull water out of skin in dry air.
the tincture is a traditional calming herb taken by mouth, with little research; on skin, colloidal oatmeal is the proven form.
Invisalign straightens; whitening comes from peroxide strips or a dentist. Skip charcoal, lemon and baking soda scrubs, which wear enamel.

title: A guide to Chinese (C-beauty) skincare brands

claims.truth: known for "morning C, evening A" (vitamin C by day, retinol by night) and its Double Resistance serum, a solid, proven pairing.
a sensitive-skin, redness-focused brand from Yunnan; its sunscreens and soothing creams are its best-known products.
brightening serums and ampoules built around pearl and niacinamide-type ingredients.
Himalayan plant masks and a niacinamide brightening line.
one of China's oldest brands (1931), now known for firming sets and, as Dr. Jenny Liu points out, a good conditioning lotion for dry ends.
red "cyclopeptide" anti-ageing sets; peptides have weak proof.

hyaluronic face mists. Two things to know: "whitening" (美白) on Chinese labels usually means evening tone and fading marks, not bleaching; the actives are niacinamide, vitamin C, arbutin and tranexamic acid. Some "whitening" creams sold online elsewhere contain mercury or hydroquinone, so buy from official flagship stores. The creator was right to wait while breastfeeding: niacinamide and azelaic acid are generally considered fine, but check with a doctor first. Bundles of 15 to 30 ampoules are a sales tactic; one bottle of the right active is enough.

title: "Hair loss deficiency": iron, biotin and growing length
body: Low iron (ferritin) really is linked to hair shedding, especially in women with heavy periods. If you shed a lot, ask your doctor for a ferritin test before taking iron (liquid iron like Floradix works, but too much iron is harmful). Results take 3 to 6 months, which matches the creator's 5 months. Biotin only helps if you're actually deficient, which is rare, and it can throw off blood tests (including heart tests), so tell your doctor if you take it. Snacks like dates, peanut butter and pumpkin seeds are good food, but they're not a hair treatment. Long natural hair is mostly length retention: gentle detangling, moisture, protective styles, low tension and patience, as the commenters say. What works on her hair may not work on yours. A hair journal (tracking wash days, products and length) is genuinely useful; you can log hair products and notes in Clay.

title: "5-product method to heal acne" and "Can I use Differin, azelaic acid and vitamin C together?"
body: All three are proven: adapalene (Differin) and azelaic acid have A-grade proof for acne, and vitamin C helps marks. Together they can work well, but not all at once from day one, especially on dry, sensitive skin. A safe way: start Differin alone, a pea-size amount 2 to 3 nights a week, over moisturiser if it stings. After 2 to 4 weeks, add azelaic acid in the mornings. Add vitamin C last, in the morning, only if your skin is calm. Moisturiser and daily sunscreen are non-negotiable. The commenter who said "one at a time" was right; the one who said "they'll ruin your skin" wasn't. Deep, painful cysts and scarring are worth a doctor's visit; prescription options work faster and prevent more scars. Any "method" with 5 steps works because it's simple and consistent, not because it's magic.

title: Buying hair, and hair "kits"

claims.truth: Reddit's advice holds: ask the vendor for unedited videos in daylight, order one bundle first, then wash and bleach-test a strand before buying more. "Raw" hair that's suspiciously cheap, or a vendor who avoids video calls, is a warning sign. Follower counts and bios like "biggest vendor" prove nothing.

(amla, bhringraj, rose and hibiscus oils, hair butter, "revival" masks): they condition and reduce breakage, so length is kept, but the "growth" claims are mostly marketing. Gentle cleansing, moisture, low tension and patience grow inches; no kit speeds up how fast hair grows.

title: Making Victoria's Secret-style mists: what the AI guides get right and wrong

claims.truth: berry, meringue, marshmallow and most fruit notes have no natural oils; they're blends of aroma chemicals (ethyl maltol for cotton candy, vanillin for vanilla, white musks for the "fluffy" feel). A ready-made fragrance oil from a soap supplier is the easy route. Perfumer's alcohol (SDA 40-B) gives a clear mist, and resting the blend for 2 days to 2 weeks really does soften it. Body mists are about 3 to 5% fragrance; eau de parfum is about 15 to 20%.

IFRA limits don't mean synthetic fragrance "won't irritate"; fragrance, natural or synthetic, is still the top cause of cosmetic allergy, so patch test. The IFRA category for body sprays is Category 4 (hydroalcoholic body and fine fragrance), not 10B, which is for household air fresheners. Some supplier oil names in those guides can't be found, so check the supplier's own site before ordering. And don't use rubbing alcohol or vodka: rubbing alcohol isn't for skin, and vodka has too much water, so the oil separates.

title: The viral "glass skin body" combo: Dove scrub plus The Ordinary peeling solution plus a glycolic spray
body: The Ordinary AHA 30% + BHA 2% is a strong 10-minute face peel. Stirred into a gritty scrub, brushed over the whole body, then followed by a glycolic toner, that's three exfoliants at once. It can cause burns, raw patches and dark marks that last for months, especially on deeper skin tones. The glowing shoulder in the photo is lighting and a filter. Better: use a scrub OR an acid on any one day, not both. Glycolic toner on the body 2 to 3 nights a week, or a lactic acid lotion for bumps, with sunscreen on exposed skin. K-beauty layering: 10 steps isn't magic. Most of those steps are watery hydrators that are fine to stack. What hurts is stacking several actives (acids, retinoids, peels, scrubs, vitamin C), which multiplies irritation. One active per routine is plenty.

title: Store products in this batch, checked

claims.claim: BCL Spa Lemon + Lily brightening mask with kojic acid
claims.truth: the lemon extract isn't a real dose of vitamin C, the lily is a moisturiser and scent, and kojic acid in a mask rinsed off after minutes barely has time to work. It's a nice moisturising spa mask, not a brightener; the leave-on niacinamide gel is the version with proof.

claims.claim: The Inkey List vs Kundal caffeine scalp serums
claims.truth: both rely on caffeine, which has weak proof (C); "10X" is marketing. If thinning is real, minoxidil is the proven option (A).

"applied to the scalp for 2 minutes" is just how to use any shampoo, "0% water" is true of every bar, and the 17 fermented herbs rinse off. Tea tree has small trials for dandruff; thuja leaf can irritate sensitive scalps. Fine if you like bars.

claims.claim: Medicube PDRN gua sha neck cream
claims.truth: PDRN's evidence is for injections, not creams; Volufiline's comes from its supplier; and collagen in a cream only moisturises. The gua sha massage briefly depuffs. For a firmer neck, a retinoid and daily sunscreen have proof.
"bio-exosome" water has no good evidence; heartleaf is soothing, and the built-in scalp brush is the nicest part.
the real deal for damaged hair. Protein treatments do strengthen bleached or heat-damaged hair for a while, so use it every 1 to 2 weeks, not every wash.

title: "Vinegar grows hair and replaces shampoo" / "Black sesame reverses greys"
body: Vinegar's acid smooths the cuticle for shine, but there's no evidence it grows hair or "tightens follicles". The "2-week microbiome reset" isn't backed by research: how much oil your scalp makes is set by hormones and genes, not by shampooing, and vinegar doesn't dissolve oil the way shampoo does, so build-up and dandruff can get worse. Aloe doesn't remove oil either; it's mostly water. Gut and scalp health may be linked, but salad dressing won't fix your hair. Black sesame: the creator is right. It's a nutritious food, but nothing shows it reverses grey hair. Roasted sesame cooking oil (the dark Japanese kind) smells strongly; for hair, use plain untoasted sesame oil. Incense cones (peony, rose, sandalwood) smell lovely, but burning them releases fine smoke particles, so burn them in a ventilated room, not every day, and keep them away from people with asthma.

title: Body oil and hair claims from this batch, checked

claims.claim: Capsaicin firms skin and helps cellulite
claims.truth: : it causes warmth and slight swelling that fade, with no lasting firming shown.

claims.claim: Clary sage and tea tree for KP and ingrowns
claims.truth: : tea tree has small studies for mild acne, but KP responds best to urea, lactic or salicylic acid.

claims.claim: Perfumed body oils make perfume last longer
claims.truth: : mostly true; scent lasts longer on moisturised skin.
: hair can't use electrolytes; it's mostly water and sugar, which helps briefly and then spoils.

: no evidence; it's just dairy fat that can soften hair before washing. The commenter is right that growth and density are mostly genetics, and heavy butters can make fine or low-porosity hair brittle or limp.
: no good trials; it coats and darkens them.

claims.claim: Charcoal is a safe, natural pigment
claims.truth: : capsule charcoal isn't made for the eye area; black iron oxide is.

title: "81% slept better with the Deep Sleep bar" / "The Bump prevents stretch marks" / "Medicinal mushroom tonics"
body: The Deep Sleep figure is a brand survey of users (no comparison group, and people expect to sleep better), not a trial. Lavender scent does have small studies for relaxation; magnesium through skin doesn't. No cream, oil or bar has been shown in good trials to prevent stretch marks; they're mostly genetic, though moisturising helps itch. Magik's CBD, ashwagandha and shiitake are in small amounts in a rinse-free butter and have no evidence for calming mood that way. Chaga and mushroom syrups are supplements, not skincare; chaga is very high in oxalates and can affect kidneys and blood thinners, so check with a doctor before taking it. Queen Helene's cleansing cream does remove makeup well, but it contains SLS, borax and six fragrance allergens, so it's not ideal for sensitive skin.

title: "Lush massage bars: worth the hype?"
body: Both sides have a point. The critics are right that they're mostly cocoa and shea butter with a little scent, so butter can mute the perfume, they pick up lint, melt in heat, and need warming before use. Store them in a tin and glide them on damp skin after a shower, where they melt instantly. On price, $15 for 2.2 oz is fair for Lush but you can make one for a few dollars (recipes for Turmeric Latte, Coconut Drench, Hayl, True Romance and Deep Sleep are in Recipes). The Deep Sleep bar's "122 mg magnesium" sounds impressive, but there's no good evidence enough passes through skin to aid sleep; the lavender scent and the massage are doing the work. Many rave reviews are paid partnerships (#ad), so weigh them accordingly. Layering a matching perfume over the bar does make scent last longer, because it clings to the oils.

title: "Dragon's blood heals cuts and zits" / "Essential-oil bug serum protects all day" / "Real plant perfumes are gentler than synthetic"
body: Mixed. Sangre de drago (Croton lechleri) does have lab and animal evidence for helping small wounds close, and its brand page has sensible safety rules; it's fine on a small, cleaned scrape. Plant oil repellents like Jungle Armor wear off within an hour or two in tests; catnip oil shows promise, but only DEET, picaridin, IR3535 and oil of lemon eucalyptus (not ordinary eucalyptus oil) are recommended where ticks or mosquito-borne disease are a risk. And natural perfumes aren't automatically gentler: rose, cinnamon, oakmoss, clove and bergamot contain some of the most common fragrance allergens, and regular bergamot can burn skin in sun. Indigo's oils and balms are nice products; homemade versions with safer swaps are in Recipes.

title: "Black sesame grows hair to the floor" / "Jasmine tea makes you smell nice from the inside out" / "Jujube protects digestion"
body: These are foods, and the claims stretch them. Black sesame is nutritious (iron, calcium, healthy fats) and traditional for greying in Chinese medicine, but no study shows it grows hair, and its phytoestrogens don't "balance hormones". Fibre doesn't make you look young. Jasmine tea doesn't change body odour; odour comes from skin bacteria breaking down sweat, so washing, antiperspirant and breathable fabric are what work. Dried jujube is a fine high-fibre snack, but the paste packets are mostly sugar. Enjoy them as food.

title: "Clinically proven to grow new hair" (New Nordic Hair Gro and Hair Volume)
body: The tocotrienol claim rests on one 2010 study of 21 people taking palm tocotrienols; hair count rose versus placebo, but it was tiny and funded by a palm oil company, and it hasn't been repeated. Apple procyanidin B2 and millet have small studies, mostly decades old. Biotin only helps people who are truly deficient, and high doses can skew blood tests (including heart and thyroid tests), so tell your doctor you take it. The shampoo's "32% more volume" comes from 34 people; rice protein coats the hair so it feels thicker, but it washes out and doesn't grow hair. For thinning, minoxidil has the real evidence; see a doctor to check iron, thyroid and hormones. The best tracking tip from the regrowth videos is sound, though: take the same three photos (part, crown, hairline) in the same spot and light each month, and judge over 3 to 6 months, not days.

title: "This salve heals cuts, cold sores and dry nasal passages" (Solve All Salve)
body: A herbal balm soothes dry, chapped skin, but the original contains comfrey, whose pyrrolizidine alkaloids can be absorbed through broken skin; comfrey products are meant for unbroken skin only. For cuts, clean them and use plain petroleum jelly. Cold sores are a virus that spreads, so use an antiviral cream from the pharmacy. Don't put essential-oil balms inside the nose. A comfrey-free version is in Recipes.

title: "Vaseline doesn't heal lips" / "Beeswax grips better" / "Licking makes lips dry ten times faster"
body: Half right. Petroleum jelly doesn't add water, but it's the best-tested occlusive (it cuts water loss by over 98% in studies) and helps the barrier repair; it isn't useless. It wears off fast because it's soft, not because it's mineral oil. The real fix is a humectant underneath (honey, glycerin, hyaluronic acid) on damp lips, sealed with the balm. Beeswax balms last longer because wax is firmer, not because they "feed" lips; shea's vitamins don't do much in a balm. Licking does dry lips through saliva enzymes and evaporation, but "ten times" is made up. Over-scrubbing makes flaking worse: once a week at most.

title: "Candie's mists are made to mix and match" / "Body mists are a skin-safe perfume"
body: Layering does work, but only because the mists share families: all three end in musk, and two have vanilla, so they bridge. The ingredient list also holds four sunscreen filters (octinoxate, oxybenzone, octisalate, avobenzone). They're there to stop light fading the colour and scent in a clear bottle, not to protect your skin; there's far too little and no SPF. Oxybenzone is one of the more common photoallergens, and mists also carry denatured alcohol and listed fragrance allergens. Spray clothes if your skin reacts. The Layer scents tool in Make shows how to build two scents up step by step.

title: "Viral K-beauty vs what works way better."
intro: Some swaps hold up, some don't.

claims.claim: Glutathione serum vs vitamin C and niacinamide pads
claims.truth: topical glutathione has little evidence; vitamin C and niacinamide (shown to fade dark spots at 4 to 5% in controlled trials) are the better bet.

claims.claim: Pore pads vs an 8% AHA essence
claims.truth: glycolic and lactic acids are well proven for rough texture, KP and dark spots, but for acne a BHA (salicylic acid) is the proven pick.

claims.claim: Centella ampoule vs a dark-spot serum
claims.truth: fair swap; centella calms and repairs, it doesn't brighten, while niacinamide, arbutin and vitamin C derivatives do.
more peptides isn't better, peptide studies are small and mostly brand-funded, and topical NAD+ is unproven. For proven anti-ageing, it's daily sunscreen and a retinoid.

madecassoside is centella's own purified active, so the real difference is that fragrance-free pads suit sensitive skin. For acne marks, redness or rosacea, azelaic acid (10 to 20%) has strong trial evidence.

title: "This 13-herb rice wine tonic stops hair fall, regrows hair and reverses greys in 60 days."
body: It's a real Vietnamese and Chinese tradition, but the claims go far beyond the evidence. Arborvitae leaf and ginseng have mouse or small studies; most of the rest (fo-ti, privet, drynaria, safflower) are traditional only. Fo-ti has caused liver injury taken by mouth, and no herb has been shown to reverse grey hair. 60 days is too short to judge regrowth anyway; hair needs 3 to 6 months. Used straight, the 65% alcohol dries the scalp. A diluted, simpler version is in Recipes.

title: "LOMA is a natural thermal protector to 450 F, with no artificial fragrance."
body: Its first three ingredients are dimethicone, trisiloxane and isoparaffin, which are silicones and a solvent; those, not the plant oils, give the heat protection. Jojoba, olive and quinoa, highlighted in the marketing, aren't in the ingredient list at all. It lists fragrance (parfum) plus coumarin, citral, limonene and linalool, so "no artificial fragrance" doesn't hold either. "Creatine is 35% more effective than any protein" has no published source. Silicones are safe and good heat protectors; the problem is calling it natural.

title: "Rosehip oil is the most concentrated source of vitamin C and fixes melasma and scars."

claims.truth: is rich in vitamin C, but vitamin C dissolves in water, so rosehip

contains almost none. The oil does have small studies for softening scars, thanks to its fatty acids and a trace of retinoic acid. It won't fix melasma, which needs sunscreen and proper treatment. "Calendula stimulates blood flow, causing a cleansing effect" isn't a real effect. Jojoba is chemically close to sebum (both contain wax esters), so that part is fair.

title: "Fo-ti, reishi and green tea block DHT" / "Ashwagandha boosts tyrosine to stop greys"
body: These come from lab dishes or animal studies, not people using the herb on their scalp. Taken by mouth, fo-ti can harm the liver and ashwagandha interacts with thyroid and sedative medicines. Better-supported herbs for skin: licorice for dark spots, centella (cica) for barrier repair, green tea for oiliness. For hair loss, minoxidil has the evidence.

title: "Body toner makes perfume last twice as long" / "Suppin is 100% safe overnight because it's skincare, not makeup"
body: Moisturised skin does hold scent longer than dry skin, but "twice as long" isn't measured; any unscented lotion or oil does the same job. Knock's 10 peptides and PDRN are mostly marketing: PDRN's evidence is for injections, not creams. As for Suppin, "skincare, not makeup" isn't a safety category. A thin oil-absorbing powder over night cream is usually fine for oily skin, but the hyaluronic acid, collagen and plant extracts are in tiny amounts, and powder doesn't stop breakouts or block dust. An SPF powder needs far more than anyone applies, so use it to top up, never as your only sunscreen. Homemade versions of both are in Recipes.

title: "Dry oil is oil-free" / "96.9% natural origin" / "Néroli is therapeutic"
body: A dry oil is 100% oil; it just absorbs fast, thanks to light oils and esters. "Natural origin" counts ingredients made from plants, including processed esters, so it says little about safety or quality. Nuxe's Néroli scent is relaxing to smell, but "therapeutic aromatherapy" is a marketing claim, and plum oil is gentle rather than proven to soothe. Homemade versions of all six are in Recipes.

title: "Self-preserving means no preservatives."
body: Not quite. Lush's linseed cream is labelled self-preserving, but its list includes drying alcohol, propylene glycol and benzyl alcohol, which together keep microbes out. Angels on Bare Skin contains water yet relies on lots of glycerin, almond and clay to keep it dry enough. A homemade copy with water and no preservative has none of that protection. Angels also contains tagetes oil, which can make skin sun-sensitive in leave-on products; in a rinse-off cleanser it is fine.

title: "If you like the Sea Breeze bar, try Lush Magic Crystals."
body: Both get their tingle from menthol and mint oils. Magic Crystals is Epsom and sea salt in a sulfate (SLES) cleanser, so it scrubs and washes at once; Sea Breeze is a plain soap bar. Neither is for the face, and salt stings fresh shaves and cuts. A homemade version is in Recipes.

title: "Sea Breeze vs Dial vs Duru: which bar soap is best?"
intro: All three are true soaps, so they clean well but sit around pH 9 to 10, higher than skin (about 5). That's fine for the body and why many people's faces feel tight after.

claims.truth: (label: palm soap base, glycerin, sorbitol, fragrance, menthol, camphor, eucalyptus and clove leaf oils, geraniol, linalool, Green 3): the tingle is menthol and camphor cooling the skin, not breaking down oil. Glycerin and sorbitol are why many find it less drying than expected. Fine for body and back; the camphor, clove and listed allergens can sting a sensitive face.

active ingredient benzalkonium chloride 0.1%. For everyday washing it hasn't been shown to beat plain soap (the FDA banned triclosan from consumer washes in 2016 and is still reviewing benzalkonium chloride). Useful for odour on underarms and feet; the dyes and fragrance allergens make it a poor face soap.

a classic palm-and-olive soap with glycerin, usually the gentlest of the three; some versions add tallow, mineral oil or fragrance allergens, so check yours. None of them "detoxes" or "melts pores": all three wash the same way and differ in fragrance, extras and how much glycerin they leave behind. For the face, a gentle syndet bar or cream cleanser is kinder; keep any of these for the body.

title: "We prefer plants over harsh steroids for eczema flare-ups."
body: Balms with butters and lipids genuinely help dry, itchy skin between flares. But used as directed, short courses of topical steroids are safe and work for active flares, and avoiding them can leave eczema untreated and infected. Many "botanical" balms also contain essential oils like manuka, which can sting and sensitize eczema skin. Use a fragrance-free balm daily and the treatment your doctor prescribes for flares.

title: "These herbs clear your skin: sarsaparilla, burdock, yellow dock, amla, Chinese skullcap."
body: These are traditional blood-purifier teas, with little human evidence for acne or eczema. Yellow dock is a laxative, burdock can lower blood sugar, and skullcap products have been linked to liver injury. Skip them in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and check with a pharmacist if you take any medication.

title: "Saffron works on all skin types, even sensitive, unlike vitamin C and acids."
body: Saffron has antioxidant compounds (crocin, safranal) and a few small studies on tone, but far less evidence than vitamin C, niacinamide or azelaic acid. Its gentleness depends on the whole formula: a saffron serum built on rose oil can carry 7 or more listed fragrance allergens, which sensitive skin often minds more than a mild acid. Grades like "Mongra" mean whole red stigmas, which matter for food color and price, not proven skin results.

title: "Gond is a collagen-boosting vegan bone broth."
body: Gond is acacia gum, a sugar-based fibre. It contains no collagen and none of the protein your body uses to build it, so it can't do what broth does. In postpartum foods like gond laddoo, the benefit is the calories, fat and warmth of the whole dish. Chinese postpartum teas (goji, red dates, longan, astragalus, codonopsis) are similar: comforting and traditional, with little direct evidence. Check herbal teas with a midwife or doctor while breastfeeding.

title: "5 mistakes to avoid with whipped body butter."
body: All five are right. Water is the big one: a water-free butter needs no preservative only while it stays dry, so a wet finger or shower splash can start mold. Use a clean spoon, keep the lid on and store it below about 24°C. If shea melts and re-sets it can turn grainy; that's texture, not spoilage. Bin it if it smells sour or crayon-like, or shows fuzzy spots.

title: "Sunscreen in a compact is so easy to reapply."
body: Handy for touch-ups, but a puff picks up very little. The SPF on the label is tested at about a quarter teaspoon for the face, and a few pats give a fraction of that. Wear a normal sunscreen in the morning and use the compact or cushion to top up.

title: "Netra Basti: a dough ring filled with warm oil soothes tired eyes."
body: It's a traditional Ayurvedic clinic treatment, where oil is pooled over open eyes. At home it can cause infection, blurred vision and irritation, and it's not safe with contact lenses, an eye condition or essential oils in the oil. For screen-tired, dry eyes, use preservative-free lubricating drops, the 20-20-20 break rule and a warm compress over closed lids. See an eye doctor if dryness persists.

title: "The power of oil: olive oil shots, castor oil packs, coconut oil pulling."
body: Olive oil is a healthy food fat, but a shot doesn't do more for skin than using it in meals. Castor oil packs feel warm and relaxing, but there's no evidence they detox anything; skip them over the belly in pregnancy and on broken skin. Oil pulling reduced plaque about as well as mouthwash in small studies, but it doesn't replace brushing and flossing. Spit the oil into the trash, not the sink.

title: "Whole bakuchi seed beats bakuchiol."
body: It's the reverse. The whole seed (babchi) contains psoralen, which causes burns, blisters and dark patches in sunlight, and psoralens are banned in EU cosmetics. Bakuchiol is extracted precisely to leave psoralen behind. The traditional vitiligo use relied on that sun reaction, under a physician. Use bakuchiol, not babchi oil or seed powder.

title: "Body oil questions everyone asks."

claims.truth: No: almond, olive, jojoba, grapeseed or fractionated coconut all work.
It's mineral oil, which works as a seal on damp skin but won't carry herbs well when infusing.
Shea is solid at room temperature, so it makes a balm, not an oil; melt it with a liquid oil for a soft butter.
Yes: warm on the lowest heat or a water bath for 1 to 2 hours, never frying.

claims.claim: Does longer infusing make it stronger?
claims.truth: Up to a few weeks with dried herbs, yes; after that it doesn't get much stronger and the oil starts to age.
Body oil softens skin; it doesn't fade dark circles, heal sunburn or erase stretch marks.
If products often sting, redden or itch, treat your skin as sensitive: patch test and skip essential oils.
Yes.

title: "Is bentonite clay the same as nzu?"
body: Both are clays, but different ones. Nzu (efun, orhue) is a soft white clay much like kaolin: gentle, cooling, good for dry or sensitive skin. Bentonite is a swelling clay that absorbs much more oil and can feel tight and drying. Swap nzu in for a gentler mask; never eat either, as some clays sold for eating contain lead.

title: "Melt-and-pour soap questions everyone asks."

claims.claim: Where do I get soap base?
claims.truth: From soap-making and skincare raw-material suppliers, craft stores, or online; look for one that lists its ingredients (glycerin, coconut-derived soap, sorbitol).
Use a double boiler: a heatproof bowl over simmering water, stirring, never boiling.
Spritz rubbing alcohol on the surface right after pouring.
A bar made from soap base doesn't; only water-based products like lotions and mists do.
Use milk powder, a teaspoon per 200 g; fresh milk can spoil and scorch.
Use skin-safe fragrance or essential oil at about 1 to 1.5%, not body spray, which has alcohol and isn't tested for skin.
Yes, a pinch for color; it won't lighten skin.
Keep it to about 1 tsp per 200 g and wrap bars.
Soap rinses off in seconds, so it can't fade stretch marks; niacinamide or salicylic acid work far better in a leave-on product than in soap.
Yes, a gentle soap suits every skin tone.

title: "It looks like a Retin-A soap, so it works like one."
body: Clear amber glycerin soaps are sold everywhere, and some carry names like Retin-A or Tretinoin. Real tretinoin is a prescription cream, and any active in a soap rinses away in seconds. Skin-lightening soaps from unregulated sellers have been found to contain mercury or steroids. Choose soaps with a full ingredient list, and get retinoids from a pharmacy.

title: "Aluminum antiperspirants cause breast cancer."
body: Large reviews by cancer agencies have found no reliable link between aluminum antiperspirants and breast cancer, and very little aluminum gets through intact skin. Aluminum salts plug sweat ducts for a while, which is why they stop wetness; aluminum-free deodorants only cover odor. Both are reasonable choices. The real reasons to skip aluminum are irritation on freshly shaved skin, or a doctor's advice if you have advanced kidney disease.

title: "Grease and pink lotion grow hair."
body: Blue Magic (petrolatum and lanolin) and Luster's Pink lotion (mineral oil and water) seal moisture in and reduce friction, so ends break less and length is kept. That shows up as "flourishing" hair over months. They don't make the scalp grow faster. Use them mostly on lengths and edges; heavy grease on the scalp can trap flakes and build up, so wash it out regularly.

title: "Eat your skincare: snow mushroom, peach gum and red dates fix dry skin."
body: These are traditional Chinese foods. Snow fungus does hold a lot of water and its extract is used in creams, but eaten, it's a gentle food like any other. "Peach gum is nature's collagen" isn't true: it's a plant gum, with no collagen at all. Papaya's vitamin C does help your body make collagen. A varied diet with enough water, fats and protein supports skin; no single food is a treatment. Black sesame and walnuts are nutritious, but there's no good evidence they reverse gray hair.

title: "Each scented powder is a different product."
body: BathTreatBakery sells over 40 dusting powders, and every one is tapioca, arrowroot, kaolin and fragrance. Merry Bath and KVK are arrowroot, kaolin, fragrance and aspen bark. The scent is the only change, and it's also the only part likely to irritate. Make one unscented base and scent small jars yourself, or keep a fragrance-free one for sensitive days. "Locks in moisture" isn't accurate: powder absorbs moisture; it's the body oil underneath that holds it.

title: "Castor oil, rice water and biotin shampoo bars grow hair."
body: A shampoo is on your scalp for under a minute. Castor oil rinses straight off, rice water can't even be in a solid bar (it would spoil), and biotin on hair does nothing; it only helps hair if you're deficient, by mouth. What these bars do well: hydrolyzed rice protein makes damaged hair feel thicker, good conditioners cut breakage, and less breakage looks like longer hair. For true thinning, minoxidil or a dermatologist.

title: "Dusting powder locks in fragrance."
body: Gourmand powders sold for scent layering (marshmallow, cinnamon, caramel) are starch plus fragrance oil. Powder over body oil does help scent stay put a little longer, but a cinnamon or pumpkin spice scent sitting on skin all day is a common cause of rashes. Choose vanilla-based blends, skip cinnamon and clove for leave-on, and use Make → Scent pairs for skin-safe amounts.

title: "Acids and kojic in a soap bar treat dark spots and texture."
body: Kitsch sells kojic acid and glycolic acid bars for dark spots. A wash is on skin for under a minute and rinsed away, so actives barely act, and fragrance (citral, linalool, limonene) comes along for the ride. They can make skin feel smoother. For spots, a leave-on azelaic acid, alpha arbutin or glycolic lotion works far better.

title: "An old brand's classic talc is the same safe formula it always was."
body: Formulas and rules change. Yardley's UK Lily of the Valley talc lists butylphenyl methylpropional (lilial), banned in UK and EU cosmetics since 2022 for possible harm to fertility, and the Indian-made tins list triclosan. Products bought through Amazon resellers can be older stock or made for other markets with different rules. Read the ingredient list on the actual tin, not the brand's reputation.

title: "Bikini brightening products are just for looks."
body: Inner-thigh and bikini darkening is usually from friction, shaving and ingrown hairs. Real actives like azelaic acid (10%) and alpha arbutin can fade it slowly over 8 to 12 weeks, and Kaia's Bikini Bright uses both. Keep them on outer skin only, never on mucous membranes, and stop if they sting. Less friction (looser clothes, anti-chafe powder) and gentler hair removal stop it coming back.

title: "Perfumed talc gives you a glowing face naturally."
body: Yardley's ads show talc on the face, but the tin is talc, chalk, magnesium carbonate, fragrance and triclosan. Powder only absorbs oil and blurs shine for a few hours; perfume on the face is a common irritant, and a cloud of talc near the nose isn't something to breathe daily. "97% naturally derived" is true because talc and chalk are mined minerals; natural-derived isn't the same as gentle. "With sun protection" on a body talc isn't a rated SPF; use real sunscreen. If you love the scent, use a starch-based powder on the body and keep perfume off the face.

title: "Honey-mustard leg wraps drain fluid, firm skin and shrink thighs."
body: Mustard heats and reddens skin by irritating it; the "circulation" is inflammation. Wrapping in film makes you sweat, so legs look a little slimmer for a few hours until you drink water again. The massage part is what helps puffy legs feel lighter, and you can do that with honey and oil, no mustard. Mustard left on skin can blister. Cellulite is how fat sits under the skin's connective bands; no wrap changes that.

title: "Body powder is the gentlest product you can use."
body: Read Lush’s powder lists closely. Sticky Dates, Sleepy Dust, Fairy Dust and Let the Good Times Roll all contain sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), which is alkaline and can sting underarms, freshly shaved skin and intimate areas. Chelsea Morning contains capsicum (chili) extract, which can burn on sensitive or shaved skin. Pochacco and Fairy Dust use cold-pressed lemon and lime oils, which can cause dark marks in the sun on leave-on skin. Most also list 8 to 13 fragrance allergens. The calmest powders are plain starch, maybe a little kaolin, and no or very little scent.

title: "Dusting powder is just a gentle, old-fashioned body treat."
body: Read the label first. Classic dusting powders like Estée Lauder Youth Dew, Prince Matchabelli Wind Song and Woods of Windsor list talc first, then perfume and a long run of fragrance allergens (Youth Dew lists 15, including oakmoss, eugenol and cinnamyl alcohol). Talc can irritate lungs when the powder clouds up, and cosmetic talc has had asbestos contamination problems. Starch-based powders (corn, tapioca, arrowroot) absorb sweat and stop chafing just as well. Don't use any loose powder near a baby's face.

title: "Occurs naturally in essential oils, so it's gentle."
body: Lush marks linalool, citral, cinnamal and coumarin with an asterisk meaning they come from essential oils. Your immune system can't tell the difference: these are the same allergens whether they come from a plant or a lab, and they're listed by law because some people react to them. Natural isn't gentler; low amounts and an unscented option are.

title: "Gift sets are the best deal."
body: L'Occitane's 6-mini hand cream set is $70 for 180 ml (about $0.39 per ml). The full 150 ml Shea Butter Hand Cream is $34 (about $0.23 per ml), and a Trader Joe's hand cream with a similar shea-and-coconut base costs a few dollars. Gift sets are good for trying scents, not for saving money. Every scented cream in the set adds a different mix of fragrance allergens, so pick one you've already tolerated.

title: "Old-fashioned beauty creams were purer."
body: Japan's Club Cosmetics sold a "medicated beauty cream" with natural female hormones in 1935, and hormone and placenta creams were common worldwide until the 1970s. Estrogen in skincare can be absorbed and affect the body, which is why it's now restricted to medicines. Heritage is a good story, not a safety standard.

title: "The $235 serum must be better than the $34 cream."
body: Read the first five ingredients. L'Occitane's $120 Immortelle Divine Face Oil starts with caprylic triglyceride and sunflower oil, two of the cheapest oils in skincare. The $235 Divine Youth serum is mostly water, propanediol and glycerin, with tiny amounts of algae extract, peptides and adenosine. The $34 Shea Hand Cream is a good, simple cream. Price follows the brand, the packaging and the story ("rare red algae that eternally regenerates"), not how well it works. For wrinkles, a retinoid and daily sunscreen beat any of them.

title: "Magic mouthwash: mix liquid Benadryl, antacid and Anbesol for a sore throat."
body: Real magic mouthwash is a prescription that a pharmacist mixes with a measured dose, usually for mouth sores from chemotherapy. The TikTok mix numbs the throat with 20% benzocaine, which can make it hard to swallow safely, and benzocaine can rarely cause methemoglobinemia (a dangerous drop in blood oxygen). Never give it to children under 2. It also adds a dose of diphenhydramine that makes you drowsy. For a sore throat, try salt-water gargles, honey and lozenges, and ask a pharmacist before mixing medicines. See a doctor if it lasts more than a week or comes with a high fever.

title: "Nature's retinol: immortelle is as effective as retinol and vitamin C."
body: L'Occitane's footnotes show what that means: 47 women for 28 days for the retinol comparison, a lab (in-vitro) test for the vitamin C one, and "100% said wrinkles looked less visible" from 33 people judging themselves. That's marketing data, not proof of equal results. The cream is a nice moisturizer with hyaluronic acid, a vitamin C derivative and oils, plus fragrance allergens (coumarin, citral, geraniol, limonene, linalool). A drugstore retinoid plus sunscreen costs far less and has decades of evidence.

title: "Drinking frankincense (luban) water helps breathing, memory and joints."
body: Boswellia extracts have some trial evidence for knee osteoarthritis, and lab studies look at anti-inflammatory compounds. Most of those used concentrated, standardized extracts in capsules, not resin soaked in water, which dissolves very little of the active acids. A glass of luban water is a pleasant tradition, not a treatment. Use only food-grade resin, skip it in pregnancy, and check with a doctor if you take blood thinners.

title: "The KIMGLOW method (ceramide, cholesterol, fatty acid) stops shedding after one wash."
body: The idea borrows the skin barrier's 3 lipids. Layering a ceramide leave-in, a cholesterol leave-in and a lanolin grease does coat and soften hair, so less of it snaps. That shows up as "less shedding" but is really less breakage. Hair falling from the root (true shedding) isn't changed by leave-ins. Three heavy layers build up, so clarify every few weeks.

title: "Biotin and peptide lash serums grow lashes like the prostaglandin ones."
body: Lash serums that clearly lengthen lashes contain prostaglandin analogs (bimatoprost, or isopropyl cloprostenate in cosmetics). They can darken eyelids and, rarely, change iris color. "Prostaglandin-free" serums with peptides, biotin and panthenol condition lashes so fewer break, but grow them much less. Rubbing biotin on lashes doesn't feed them.

title: "Grocery-store skincare is a dupe of the luxury brand."
body: Sometimes it really is close: Trader Joe's original hand cream shares the shea-and-coconut base of L'Occitane's, for a fraction of the price. Compare ingredient lists, not packaging. Watch the scented editions, which add fragrance allergens (coumarin, cinnamal, eugenol), and remember a 0.3% retinol is a gentle starter, not a stronger product.

title: "Mango leaf vinegar penetrates the roots and stops greys."
body: Mangiferin is a real antioxidant, but a rinse sits on the scalp for minutes and can't reverse greying or boost follicle circulation. Diluted vinegar does smooth the cuticle and adds shine. Dilute 1 part to at least 4 parts water, rinse it out, and keep it out of the eyes.

title: "Sida acuta and ewedu are the same hair-wash leaf."
body: They look alike but are different plants. Ewedu (jute leaf, mrenda, molokhia) is a food leaf that turns slippery and detangles hair. Sida acuta ("broomweed") is a different herb. Buy from someone who can name the plant, and patch test any leaf on your scalp first.

title: "Splurge or save? Check before you buy."
body: Will you use it 3 or more times a week? Does it list a proven active at a known strength? Is there a cheaper match with the same active (try Find a cheaper match)? Could you make the base yourself (oils, butters, scrubs) and buy only the active? If you're unsure, wishlist it for a month; most impulse buys don't survive.

title: "Red clay boosts circulation and cell renewal."
body: Red clay gets its colour from iron oxide and is a gentle, mid-strength clay. A clay mask can bring a temporary flush and leaves skin feeling smooth, but it doesn't renew cells or improve circulation in any lasting way. Rinse before it dries, and kaolin is still gentler for very sensitive skin.

title: "Beef tallow is the ancient secret for glowing skin."
body: Tallow is a rich, skin-like fat that seals in moisture well, much like shea or lanolin. Its vitamins A, D, E and K are in small amounts; it isn't a retinoid. It can clog pores on acne-prone faces, goes rancid and smells, and isn't suited to eczema flares without a doctor's plan. Fine as a body or lip balm if you like it; a ceramide cream does the same barrier job, tested.

title: "Volcanic ash clay detoxes skin from the inside out."
body: Volcanic clay absorbs oil and surface grime like any clay. It can't pull toxins from inside the body, and its minerals don't feed your skin. Rinse it off before it cracks dry, once or twice a week, and moisturize after.

title: "Mongongo oil forms a UV-protective film."
body: Mongongo (manketti) is a lovely light oil for skin and hair. Its eleostearic acid does react to UV, but no oil gives tested sun protection. Wear real SPF over it.

title: "Myrrh oil treats gum disease, thyroid problems, anxiety and nail fungus."
body: Myrrh smells warm and is traditional in mouth rinses at tiny, diluted amounts. It shouldn't go neat on gums or skin, and rubbing it over your thyroid does nothing for thyroid function; see a doctor for that, and for depression, bronchitis or fungal nails. Not for use in pregnancy.

title: "A body oil with niacinamide, peptides and hyaluronic acid works like a serum."
body: Body oils like Truly Birthday Sex list water-loving actives that don't dissolve in oil, so they're likely there in token amounts. Enjoy it for shimmer and scent. For real body results, a lotion with niacinamide or lactic acid does more.

title: "Bath teas are always gentler than bath bombs."
body: Bath teas skip fizz, dye and glitter, which suits sensitive skin. But plants can still irritate (ragweed-family flowers like chamomile, for example), and "no synthetic fragrance" doesn't make essential oils gentler. Both are fine for most people; rinse the tub after either.

title: "Rosehip oil fades scars, dark spots and wrinkles."
body: Rosehip is a lovely light oil rich in fatty acids, and it does help dry, rough skin. Its vitamin C mostly doesn't survive pressing, and the tiny natural trans-retinoic acid in it isn't enough to work like a retinoid. For dark spots and fine lines, daily sunscreen plus tested actives (azelaic acid, niacinamide, retinoids) do much more. It goes rancid quickly: buy small, keep it cool and dark.

title: "A 10-minute Epsom foot soak detoxes and boosts endorphins."
body: The real benefit is ten quiet minutes, warmth and putting your feet up, which genuinely helps you unwind. Feet don't release toxins into the water, and skin absorbs very little magnesium. Skip hot soaks if you have diabetes or numb feet, and dry well between the toes.

title: "DIY toilet bombs clean the toilet."
body: Baking soda and citric acid fizz, which is fun and freshens the smell, but the fizz cancels both out, so they barely clean. A brush and regular toilet cleaner do the work. Never mix them with bleach cleaners, and keep the jar away from kids, since they look like candy.

title: "Homemade scent balls in the toilet tank keep the house fresh."
body: Soap, baking soda, fabric softener and rubbing alcohol balls are fine in a drawer or shoe box. Don't put them in the toilet tank: dissolving soap and residue can damage the flapper and fill valve and void warranties. They mask odors; baking soda absorbs only a little.

title: "Lash and brow serums with rosemary, nettle and castor oil grow lashes."
body: Castor oil conditions lashes so they look glossier, but no herb oil has good evidence for growing lashes. Keep essential oils well away from the eyes. Prescription bimatoprost (Latisse) is the only proven lash grower and has side effects worth asking a doctor about.

title: "Brightening soaps with kojic acid, licorice or vitamin C fade dark spots."
body: A pretty soap collection labelled "fades dark spots" still rinses off within a minute. Charcoal and lemon don't detox, and vitamin C breaks down in soap. Choose a soap you like, and put leave-on actives and sunscreen to work on spots.

title: "Menopause cooling oils treat hot flashes."
body: Menthol, peppermint and camphor give a real cooling feeling for a few minutes, which can be comforting. They don't change hormones or how often flashes happen. Comfrey and arnica oils are for unbroken skin only; St. John's wort oil can make skin sun-sensitive. Talk to a doctor about treatments that reduce hot flashes.

title: "Butterfly pea and collagen gels boost your collagen."
body: Collagen in a gel is too large to reach the deeper skin; it holds water on the surface like glycerin. Butterfly pea adds color and antioxidants. Real collagen support comes from daily sunscreen and retinoids, then vitamin C.

title: "Petroleum lip balm is toxic and beeswax balm scores 92."
body: Scanner-app scores like this aren't safety ratings. Cosmetic petroleum jelly is highly purified, one of the least allergenic ingredients, and seals lips better than almost anything. The "car wax" in balms is carnauba, a palm leaf wax; "candle wax" is cosmetic-grade paraffin. Real trade-offs: camphor and fragrance can irritate dry lips, and beeswax or lanolin can cause allergies in a few people. Pick what your lips like.

title: "Scrubs fade cellulite, remove tan and boost circulation."
body: Sugar, salt and coffee scrubs smooth rough skin and make it look brighter for a day. Cellulite is structural, under the skin; a tan fades as skin renews; and any circulation boost lasts minutes. Scrub 1 to 2 times a week at most and follow with moisturizer.

title: "Mineral toothpaste strengthens enamel naturally."
body: Calcium carbonate, clay and baking soda polish teeth and freshen breath, and xylitol helps against cavity bacteria. Without fluoride, though, nothing in a DIY paste rebuilds enamel or prevents cavities; fluoride is what does that. Use DIY powders as an extra, a few times a week. Keep xylitol away from dogs.

title: "Breast milk lotion and bum cream are the gentlest thing for a baby."
body: Breast milk is wonderful to drink and fine in a fresh bath or a small amount in soap. Whisked into oils and stored, it has no preservative and grows bacteria within days, then goes onto broken diaper skin. For diaper rash, a plain zinc oxide or petrolatum cream is safer. No essential oils under 3 months.

title: "Detox soap pulls toxins from your skin."
body: Charcoal, clay, spirulina and sea salt in a soap help it feel deep-cleaning and look striking. Soap rinses off in seconds and skin doesn't store toxins for it to pull out. Enjoy it as a nice bar. Bergamot or lime oil is fine here because it rinses off.

title: "Pick a shampoo by curl type."
body: Your scalp matters more: oily scalps need washing more often and suit clarifying shampoos; dry or sensitive scalps do better with gentle, fragrance-free ones. Then pick conditioner and leave-ins by hair texture and porosity. Hyaluronic acid in shampoo rinses off. Parabens are safe, well-studied preservatives; sulfates are fine unless your hair or scalp feels dry. Coconut oil in shampoo makes some low-porosity hair stiff.

title: "Kokum, shea, mango and cocoa butter all do the same thing."
body: They all seal in moisture, but they feel different. Kokum is hard and dry-feeling and rarely clogs pores, good for faces and lip balms. Shea is soft and rich. Mango is creamy and in between. Cocoa is very hard, smells of chocolate and can clog pores on the face. Pick by texture and where you'll use it.

title: "Brightening soap with niacinamide or arbutin fades dark spots."
body: Brands like Haps Beauty sell brightening soaps and "glass skin" washes with clinical-sounding actives. In a wash, those actives rinse away within a minute. Spend on a cheap gentle cleanser, then put the money into a leave-on niacinamide, azelaic acid or arbutin product and daily sunscreen. Watch for fragrance and sulfates in bars sold for sensitive skin.

title: "Brightening soap fades dark spots."
body: Soap is on your skin for under a minute, then rinsed away. Letting the lather sit 1 to 2 minutes helps a little, but can also irritate, especially underarms or after shaving. Kojic acid dipalmitate is gentler than plain kojic acid. Vitamin C breaks down in soap. Turmeric calms skin, but it stains. Leave-on products work better: azelaic acid, niacinamide, alpha arbutin or tranexamic acid. Kojic acid doesn't make skin sun-sensitive the way retinol and acids do, but sun darkens spots again, so sunscreen still decides your results.

title: "A coffee mask lightens underarms and dark skin."
body: Coffee, besan, yogurt and turmeric make a nice softening mask. Caffeine can briefly de-puff, and gentle exfoliation makes skin look fresher. None of it lightens skin. Underarm darkening usually comes from friction, shaving or irritation, so gentle hair removal, loose fabric and leave-on actives help more. "Apply on damp skin, absorbs 10x better" is half true: damp skin helps moisturizers hold water, but it doesn't make a rinse-off mask work harder.

title: "Influencers' results come only from homemade recipes."
body: Many also use dermatologist treatments and store-bought actives, and good lighting and genetics help too. DIY is good for gentle basics like cleansing masks, oils, balms and scrubs. Dark spots, acne and hair loss usually need tested actives or a doctor.

title: "Batch your wash-and-go styler cocktail with water."
body: Mixing gel, mousse and a little grease (like Blue Magic) with water is fine for one wash day. Stored, the water dilutes each product's preservative and the mix can grow mold within days. Mix only what you need, in a clean bowl, each time. More water means softer and more moisture; more gel means more hold, which helps in humid weather.

title: "You have to choose between a hair tonic and a scalp serum."
body: Use both if you like. A tonic is watery and light: it refreshes the scalp and balances oil, and you can use it daily. A serum is thicker and more concentrated for one concern, like itch, a weak barrier or thinning. Apply the tonic first, then the serum, on a clean scalp. Choose tonics by scalp type (tea tree for oily, rosemary for dry, mild formulas for sensitive). Neither replaces minoxidil for hereditary thinning.

title: "Korean hair products don't work on Black hair."
body: Hair care works by what your scalp and strands need, not where a product is made. Choose by scalp first (oily, dry, flaky or sensitive decides how often you wash), then by hair condition and porosity. Low porosity: lighter, water-based leave-ins and mists, with gentle heat under a cap so a mask spreads. High porosity or damaged: richer masks and a leave-in, sealed with oil on the ends. Creators like seonnej use brands such as Aromatica, Dr.FORHAIR, Mise en Scène, Unove and MoAC this way.

title: "Protein in a weekly shampoo will make hair brittle."
body: Hydrolyzed proteins in a rinse-off shampoo are a small amount on your hair for a minute; they're fine weekly for most people. "Protein overload" (stiff, straw-like hair) is more likely from frequent protein treatments or bond masks layered on top. If hair feels stiff, swap one wash for a moisturizing, protein-free conditioner.

title: "A peptide hair mist makes hair grow stronger, fuller and longer."
body: Note the small print: "longer looking". Peptide and caffeine scalp mists have mostly brand-funded studies and work more as conditioners and scalp comfort products. What really makes hair look fuller is keeping what you grow: gentle detangling, a satin bonnet, low-tension styles, little heat, and a clean scalp, as Derly herself says. For true thinning, minoxidil is the proven option, and a doctor can check iron, vitamin D and thyroid.

title: "One professional peel corrected her pigmentation."
body: Before-and-after photos of depigmentation peels (like Cosmelan) leave out the months of home cream, strict daily sunscreen and the redness and peeling in between. They can help melasma and dark marks when done by a trained professional, but on deeper skin tones the wrong peel can cause worse dark patches. Ask about their experience with your skin tone, and start with sunscreen and azelaic acid or niacinamide at home.

title: "Waxing direction doesn't matter."
body: It does: spread wax in the direction the hair grows and pull it off quickly against it, low and close to the skin, keeping the skin taut. On the backs of legs hair often grows at an angle, so follow it. This means less breakage, fewer ingrowns and less pain. Muslin or cloth strips can be washed and reused with sugar wax.

title: "4C hair needs a daily moisture routine and a shelf full of products."
body: A low-effort routine works well for many people with 4C coils: every 1 to 3 weeks, wash and detangle under running water with a slippery conditioner, finger-detangling or using a wide-tooth comb; then seal damp hair once with a butter or oil and put it into 4 to 6 chunky twists or braids. Daily, just wear a satin bonnet or scarf. Coiled hair sheds 50 to 100 hairs a day like everyone's, but shed hairs get trapped in the coils, so detangle regularly to avoid matting. Wash more often if your scalp itches or flakes. Drugstore picks like tgin, As I Am and Mielle do the job.

title: "French pharmacy creams fix everything in one tube."
body: Some deserve the hype, with caveats. Azelaic acid 15% (ACM Azéane) helps dark spots, acne and rosacea redness, but takes 2 to 3 months and can tingle. 30% urea (Eucerin) is excellent for heels, calluses and bumpy skin, but too strong for the face. Glycolic acid plus retinal in one cream (Avène Cleanance Comedomed Peeling) is effective but irritating: start every 2 to 3 nights and wear sunscreen. Cica barrier creams soothe chapped skin but don't heal wounds. A score of 9999/10 is enthusiasm, not evidence.

title: "Refills are always the greener choice."
body: Refill pouches, like Torriden's or Josie Maran's, usually use far less plastic than a new bottle, so they are a good habit. Keep the original pump clean and dry before refilling, pour carefully to avoid getting water in, and don't top up old product with new; finish it first.

title: "Japanese drugstore shampoos are gentler because they're Japanese."
body: Brands like Moist Diane, &honey and Kracie Ichikami are well-made and often lovely to use, with silicones and conditioning agents for smooth, shiny hair. They're cleansers like any other; choose by scent, feel and whether your hair likes silicones. Same goes for any shampoo sold as "Ayurvedic growth": it washes, it doesn't grow hair.

title: "Sleeping in loose hair or skipping washes in protective styles is fine."
body: A small hair brand's tips hold up: tie hair in a loose style and use a satin bonnet or pillowcase to cut friction and breakage overnight, and keep washing your scalp in braids and extensions, about every 1 to 2 weeks, to prevent buildup and itch. Flaxseed gel or a slippery conditioner makes detangling easier on wash day.

title: "Rare African botanicals are scientifically proven to repair and firm skin."
body: Oils like ximenia, mongongo, safou, kpangnan and mafura are genuinely lovely emollients with long traditional use, and supporting women's co-ops that harvest them matters.
